9.3. Minimization and Variations🔗

9.3.1. The Direct Method🔗

9.3.1.1. From an Infimum to a Minimizer🔗

The direct method proves a minimizer exists without ever writing one down. You start with a sequence (u_k) satisfying

J(u_k)\longrightarrow\inf_{v\in A}J(v),

where A is the admissible class. The sequence need not converge strongly, and its limit need not be available in closed form. The proof instead chooses a topology weak enough to provide compactness and strong enough for the energy to survive passage to the limit.

The old Dirichlet principle assumed that an energy infimum was attained and then used the minimizer to solve a boundary-value problem. Weierstrass's objections exposed the missing existence argument: continuity alone on an infinite-dimensional function space does not force an infimum to be attained. Hilbert, Tonelli, and later Morrey supplied conditions under which the principle becomes valid. Evans's Chapter 8 presents the modern Sobolev-space argument through weak convergence, coercivity, and lower semicontinuity.

In a reflexive space, the argument has the following form:

\text{coercivity} \longrightarrow\text{bounded minimizing sequence} \longrightarrow\text{weakly convergent subsequence} \longrightarrow\text{weak lower semicontinuity} \longrightarrow\text{minimizer}.

The panels isolate two parts of the argument. The scalar energy shows how coercivity confines a minimizing sequence. The oscillating functions explain why we may need weak convergence: their norms do not decay, even though their pairing with the displayed test function tends to zero. That one pairing illustrates the distinction; weak convergence requires the corresponding limit against every continuous linear functional.

Coercivity prevents escape to infinity. If

\lVert u\rVert\longrightarrow\infty \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J(u)\longrightarrow+\infty,

then every sufficiently low sublevel set is bounded. Reflexivity turns that bound into a weakly convergent subsequence. Weak closedness keeps the limit inside A, and weak lower semicontinuity gives

J(u)\leq\liminf_{j\to\infty}J(u_{k_j}) =\inf_{v\in A}J(v).

9.3.1.2. Compactness and Lower Semicontinuity🔗

A convex functional that is lower semicontinuous in norm is weakly lower semicontinuous. Strict convexity adds uniqueness; existence does not need it.

9.3.1.3. Concrete Energies🔗

For a quadratic L^2 energy, expanding a squared norm gives these properties directly. For integral functionals

I(u)=\int_\Omega L(x,u(x),Du(x))\,dx

the hypotheses have to be derived from properties of the density L.

For a complete real Hilbert space H, the canonical isometric map

\iota_H:H\longrightarrow(H^*)^*,\qquad \iota_H(x)(\ell)=\ell(x),

is surjective. Thus H is reflexive in the functional-analytic sense used by the direct method.

    The canonical map from a real Hilbert space into its continuous double dual is surjective. This is the reflexivity of Hilbert spaces, proved by pulling a double-dual functional back along the Riesz isometry.

Proof for Theorem 9.88
uses 0

Pull a double-dual functional back along the Fréchet–Riesz isometric equivalence between the Hilbert space and its continuous dual. Applying the inverse equivalence produces a vector whose canonical double-dual image is the original functional.

Reflexivity feeds the compactness statements: it identifies the weak topology of H with the weak-star topology of its double dual, where Banach–Alaoglu applies. The norm-bound and Radon–Riesz estimates use something more elementary, namely the defining property of weak convergence.

Proof for Theorem 9.89
uses 0

The weak topology on H is the initial topology generated by all continuous linear functionals \ell:H\to\mathbb R. Therefore each evaluation map is continuous by construction. Applying that continuity to x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x gives \ell(x_\alpha)\to\ell(x) for every \ell\in H^*.

Reflexivity and Banach–Alaoglu give the compactness half of the direct method: a norm bound on a minimizing sequence, together with weak closedness of the sublevel set it lives in, is enough to produce a weak cluster point.

A weakly closed subset of a complete real Hilbert space is weakly compact when its underlying normed-space set is bounded:

K\subset H,\qquad K\ \text{weakly closed and norm bounded} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K\ \text{weakly compact}.

The Lean theorem is stated for Mathlib's weak-space topology and proves topological compactness.

Proof for Theorem 9.90
uses 1

Hilbert reflexivity identifies the weak space with the range of its canonical weak-star double-dual embedding. Banach–Alaoglu gives compactness of the bounded weak-star closure, and the embedding transfers compactness back to the weak topology. Weak closedness removes the closure operation.

Compactness of a sublevel set does not by itself keep a weak limit inside a constrained admissible class. For linear constraints, weak continuity of the constraint maps does.

Theorem 9.88
Loading preview
Group member preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.
uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let A_j:H\to K be any family of continuous linear maps. Their simultaneous kernel

\mathcal C=\bigcap_j\ker A_j

is weakly closed. Consequently, if x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x and, eventually, A_jx_\alpha=0 for all j simultaneously, then A_jx=0 for every j. If S\subset H is weakly closed and norm bounded, then S\cap\mathcal C is weakly compact.

The same argument preserves, under weak limits, incompressibility, zero mean, homogeneous traces, and other linear PDE side conditions once the relevant operators are continuous.

Proof for Theorem 9.91
uses 1

Every continuous linear map A_j is continuous from the weak topology of H to the weak topology of K: composing a continuous functional on K with A_j gives a continuous functional on H. Hence each kernel is weakly closed, and arbitrary intersections preserve closedness. A weak limit that is eventually in this intersection remains in it. Finally, intersecting with a weakly closed bounded set preserves closedness and boundedness, so Hilbert weak compactness applies.

A weak limit produced by compactness comes with no size information of its own. The evaluation property supplies it, and in the direct method this keeps the minimizer inside the same ball as the minimizing sequence.

In any real normed space, if x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x and eventually \lVert x_\alpha\rVert\leq C, then

\lVert x\rVert\leq C.

This is the bounded-net form of weak lower semicontinuity of the norm; neither completeness nor reflexivity is needed.

    Weak lower semicontinuity of the norm in a real normed space: if uᵢ ⇀ w weakly and eventually ‖uᵢ‖ ≤ C, then ‖w‖ ≤ C. The proof tests against a norming functional at w given by Hahn–Banach.

Proof for Theorem 9.92
uses 1

Hahn–Banach supplies a continuous linear functional \ell with \lVert\ell\rVert\leq1 and \ell(x)=\lVert x\rVert. The eventual norm bound gives \ell(x_\alpha)\leq C. Weak convergence passes this inequality to the limit, yielding \lVert x\rVert\leq C. The norming-functional statement also covers x=0.

Norm can be lost in a weak limit, as an orthonormal sequence tending weakly to zero shows. The Radon–Riesz property says that this loss is the only obstruction to strong convergence.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Weak convergence in a real Hilbert space, together with convergence of the norms to the norm of the weak limit, implies strong convergence:

x_\alpha\rightharpoonup x,\qquad \lVert x_\alpha\rVert\longrightarrow\lVert x\rVert \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lVert x_\alpha-x\rVert\longrightarrow0.

We use this Radon–Riesz property of Hilbert spaces when an energy identity upgrades a weakly obtained limit or trace to norm convergence.

    Radon–Riesz property: in a real inner product space, weak convergence together with convergence of norms implies norm convergence.

Proof for Theorem 9.93
uses 1

Expand the squared distance:

\|x_\alpha-x\|^2 =\|x_\alpha\|^2+\|x\|^2-2\langle x_\alpha,x\rangle.

Weak convergence gives \langle x_\alpha,x\rangle\to\langle x,x\rangle, while the additional norm hypothesis gives \|x_\alpha\|^2\to\|x\|^2. All three terms are now controlled, and their limit is zero. For an orthonormal sequence the mixed term still converges, but the squared norms stay at one; that is precisely the missing hypothesis.

uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

A weakly lower-semicontinuous real functional on a complete real Hilbert space attains a global minimum if the sublevel through some supplied x_0\in H is norm bounded:

\{x\in H:J(x)\leq J(x_0)\} \quad\text{is norm bounded}.

Then there is u\in H such that J(u)\leq J(v) for every v\in H. This is the compactness-plus-liminf core of the direct method.

    A weakly lower semicontinuous functional on a real Hilbert space attains its global minimum if one of its nonempty sublevel sets is norm bounded.

Proof for Theorem 9.94
uses 1

The sublevel through x_0 is weakly closed by lower semicontinuity, weakly compact by boundedness, and nonempty because it contains x_0. The functional therefore attains a minimum there. That minimum is at most J(x_0), while every point outside the sublevel has larger energy, so the constrained minimum is global.

The bounded-sublevel hypothesis must be checked at a specific point x_0; coercivity removes that bookkeeping.

then J has a global minimizer.

uses 1

Both existence theorems assume lower semicontinuity for the weak topology, a hypothesis that is awkward to verify directly because weakly convergent nets need not converge in norm. Convexity is the standard way to obtain it from the norm topology.

Every convex real functional on a real normed space that is lower semicontinuous in norm is lower semicontinuous for the weak topology:

Proof for Theorem 9.96
uses 0

For every real a, the sublevel \{x:J(x)\leq a\} is convex because J is convex and norm closed because J is norm lower semicontinuous. A norm-closed convex set is weakly closed by Hahn–Banach separation. Thus every sublevel is weakly closed, which is equivalent to lower semicontinuity of J in the weak topology.

Combined with the coercive existence theorem, this criterion removes the weak topology from the hypotheses. Completeness of H is still required, since the weak compactness theorem uses it.

Proof for Theorem 9.100
uses 0

Mathlib's L² inner-product formula identifies the integral of the pointwise squared norm with the Hilbert norm squared.

Once J_f is the squared distance to f, convexity is inherited from the squared norm of an inner-product space, which satisfies the exact identity

\lVert(1-t)u+tv\rVert^2 =(1-t)\lVert u\rVert^2+t\lVert v\rVert^2-t(1-t)\lVert u-v\rVert^2 \qquad(0\leq t\leq1);

translation by f leaves the correction term unchanged.

Proof for Theorem 9.102
uses 0

The squared-distance formula gives strong continuity, while strong convexity gives convexity. The theorem on closed convex sublevel sets then gives weak lower semicontinuity.

Weak lower semicontinuity is one of the two direct-method inputs; coercivity is the other. For a squared distance it is immediate, since J_f(u) is at least (\lVert u\rVert-\lVert f\rVert)^2 and so grows like \lVert u\rVert^2 once \lVert u\rVert is large.

9.3.1.7. Sobolev Integral Functionals🔗

9.3.1.7.1. Convex integral functionals on Sobolev space🔗

9.3.1.7.1.1. Finding a field by minimizing its energy🔗

For integral functionals there are two existence results. The Hilbert-space criterion treats the whole space. The mixed-energy theorem constructs a minimizer in a fixed affine class g+W^{1,p}_0(\Omega); it allows infinite energies and starts from one finite-energy competitor.

Finding a minimizer and identifying its equation are separate steps. For a differentiable functional, the first derivative vanishes along a variation when both signs of that variation are admissible. Computing that derivative gives the weak Poisson equation in our example. For mixed densities, the first-variation theorem derives the directional formula from growth of the supplied full density derivative.

9.3.1.7.1.2. The concrete picture🔗

Here H^1(\Omega) is the weak-derivative graph space. On an open domain it is the Sobolev space used by Evans; on an arbitrary set the theorems are statements about the graph space, and open-domain Sobolev results keep their openness hypothesis.

    The pointwise first-order jet (u(x), Du(x)) of a scalar H¹ field.

    The first component is the canonical L² representative of u; the second is the finite Euclidean vector of canonical representatives of its first weak derivatives.

The jet is exactly the argument that a first-order density F(x,z,p) takes, with z=u(x) and p=Du(x). Integrating the composite over \Omega against the domain measure defines the functional whose minimizers are sought.

    The scalar first-order integral functional of Evans, §8.2.1, equation (1):

    J_F(u) = ∫_Ω F(x, u(x), Du(x)) dx.

    The second argument of F bundles the scalar value and Euclidean weak gradient as (u(x), Du(x)). This definition uses Mathlib's totalized Bochner integral. Quadratic growth gives integrability below; more general densities require a separate integrability hypothesis for integral order arguments.

Mathlib's Bochner integral assigns zero to a nonintegrable density. Before using J_F as an energy, we therefore need integrability for the fields under consideration.

A quadratic-growth theorem gives one way to prove this. Suppose F is jointly measurable and, for almost every x and every (z,p),

|F(x,z,p)|\leq a(x)+C\max\{|z|,\|p\|\}^2, \qquad a\in L^1(\Omega),\quad C\geq0.

The maximum is the product norm on \mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n. Since its square is at most |z|^2+\|p\|^2, evaluating this bound at (u(x),Du(x)) gives an integrable majorant for every u\in H^1(\Omega). The canonical representatives agree with the L^2 coordinates almost everywhere, which suffices for this integral estimate.

This establishes finiteness of the energy without convexity or a bounded domain. Convexity is the next input: it passes from F(x,-,-) to the integral because the jet map respects affine combinations almost everywhere. The convexity theorem keeps integrability as a hypothesis so that other growth conditions can supply it too.

Proof for Theorem 9.108
uses 0

The canonical representatives of (1-t)u+tv agree almost everywhere with the same affine combination of the representatives of u and v, both in the base coordinate and every weak-derivative coordinate. Apply pointwise convexity of F(x,-,-) to these jets for almost every x, then integrate the resulting inequality. Linearity of the integral gives the stated convex combination of energies.

Convexity is what connects the integral functional to the weak topology.

Suppose F(x,-,-) is jointly convex for almost every x, every admissible density F(x,u(x),Du(x)) is integrable, and the resulting functional is lower semicontinuous in the strong H^1 topology. Then

u_\alpha\rightharpoonup u\ \text{in }H^1(\Omega) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_F(u)\leq\liminf_\alpha J_F(u_\alpha).

This Hilbert-space criterion takes strong lower semicontinuity as an input. A second result derives sequential lower semicontinuity from convexity in the gradient variable, using strong convergence of the values.

On a finite measure space, let 1<p<\infty and write the density as F(x,s,z), with s\in\mathbb R and z\in\mathbb R^n. Assume that F, its gradient derivative D=\partial_zF, and a spatial lower bound a(x) are measurable in their indicated variables. For almost every x, assume that F(x,s,z) and D(x,s,z) are continuous in s for each fixed z, that F(x,s,\cdot) is convex and differentiable for every s, and that F(x,s,z)\geq a(x) for all s,z.

If v_j\to v strongly in L^p, while z_j\rightharpoonup z weakly in L^p with \sup_j\|z_j\|_p<\infty, then

\int \bigl(F(x,v,z)-a(x)\bigr)\,d\mu \leq\liminf_j\int \bigl(F(x,v_j,z_j)-a(x)\bigr)\,d\mu.

These are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals with values in [0,\infty]. There is no upper growth bound on F or D, and a need only be measurable. An integrable a makes this a finite constant shift of the original energy. The Lean theorem also permits the values to converge strongly in a different L^r space, 1\leq r\leq\infty.

When z ranges over a finite-dimensional space, as the gradient of a Sobolev function does, the derivative D is not needed. The same inequality holds for every measurable F such that, for almost every x, F(x,s,z) is continuous in s for each z, convex in z for each s, and at least a(x). These are the Carathéodory integrands that are convex in the gradient.

    On a finite measure space, an integral energy whose density is continuous in the value for each gradient, convex in the gradient and bounded below by a function b of the point is lower semicontinuous under almost-everywhere convergence of the values and weak Lᵖ convergence of the gradients, for a finite conjugate exponent q. Theorem 9.96
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

For the Hilbert-space criterion, pointwise convexity and integrability give convexity of the integral functional. Closed convex sublevel sets then upgrade strong lower semicontinuity to weak lower semicontinuity.

For the sequential result, first choose indices tending to infinity along which the energies tend to their liminf. Strong convergence of the values allows a further selection converging almost everywhere. Convexity in z gives a supporting affine function at the limiting gradient. Restrict to measurable sets on which these supporting densities and fields are uniformly bounded. Continuity in s and dominated convergence give strong L^{p'} convergence of the restricted fields, where p'=p/(p-1)<\infty. Pairing them with the bounded, weakly convergent gradients passes the affine inequality to the limit. Fatou's lemma removes the restriction to those sets. The proof never requires a global integrable bound on the supporting field.

For the form without a derivative, continuity in s and convexity in z first give continuity in the pair (s,z). Replace F(x,s,\cdot) by its Moreau envelope F_\lambda(x,s,z)=\inf_w\bigl(F(x,s,w)+|w-z|^2/(2\lambda)\bigr). It is convex and differentiable in z, it and its gradient are continuous in s, and a\leq F_\lambda\leq F. The differentiable form applies to F_\lambda and bounds \int(F_\lambda(x,v,z)-a) by the liminf for F. As \lambda decreases to 0, F_\lambda increases to F, and monotone convergence gives the inequality for F.

The Hilbert-space criterion assumes coercivity. For a mixed density with a positive lower bound in the gradient, Poincaré derives the corresponding bound on the admissible sublevel.

Pointwise convexity, density integrability, strong lower semicontinuity, and coercivity give

\exists u\in H^1(\Omega),\qquad J_F(u)=\inf_{v\in H^1(\Omega)}J_F(v).

This first conclusion is unconstrained. The mixed-energy result works in a prescribed affine class. Let n\geq1, let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be bounded and measurable, and let 1<p<\infty. Assume that F is measurable and that, for almost every x\in\Omega, F(x,s,z) is continuous in s for each z and convex in z for each s. No derivative in z is assumed. Suppose that b:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is measurable and that, for some c>0, almost every x satisfies

F(x,s,z)\geq c|z|^p-b(x)\qquad\text{for every }s\in\mathbb R,\ z\in\mathbb R^n.

For g\in W^{1,p}(\Omega), set \mathcal A=g+W^{1,p}_0(\Omega) and define

J_b^+(u)=\int_\Omega\bigl(F(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))+b(x)\bigr)\,dx \in[0,\infty].

If one v_0\in\mathcal A has J_b^+(v_0)<\infty, there is a u\in\mathcal A such that

J_b^+(u)<\infty,\qquad J_b^+(u)\leq J_b^+(v)\quad\text{for every }v\in\mathcal A.

The lower bound is uniform in the value s. It makes the shifted density nonnegative, so the energy is a nonnegative Lebesgue integral even when some competitors have infinite energy. No upper growth bound is required. If b is integrable, this also minimizes the original extended energy after subtracting the finite constant \int_\Omega b. On measurable sets, W^{1,p}_0 means the supported smooth-core closure; on open sets it is the usual zero-boundary space. No boundary atlas is assumed.

Here 1 < p < ∞, the domain is bounded and measurable, and its dimension is positive.     Convexity concerns only the gradient, and no derivative of the density is assumed. The density is measurable and continuous in the value variable almost everywhere. The displayed functional adds the spatial lower bound b; if b is integrable, this is a finite constant shift of the original energy. Uniform constant lower bounds are a special case on these bounded domains.

For the unconstrained Hilbert result, the Sobolev integral theorem supplies weak lower semicontinuity, and the coercive direct method attains the infimum.

For the affine result, write each competitor as g+w with w\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega). The gradient lower bound and Poincaré control the W^{1,p} norm of corrections in the sublevel below the finite competitor. Reflexivity and separability give a weakly convergent subsequence of a minimizing sequence in this closed Sobolev subspace. Compactness of its base coordinate gives strong L^p convergence of the values; adding the fixed field g preserves that convergence. The gradients remain bounded and converge weakly along the same subsequence. Apply the preceding sequential inequality, in its form without a derivative, with a=-b. The limit stays in the affine class and its energy is no larger than the infimum approached by the sequence, hence it minimizes. Comparison with the finite competitor makes its energy finite.

The exponential-energy example gives a different reason to use the extended integral. On a bounded measurable \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n, n\geq1, consider

E(u)=\int_\Omega\left(e^{|\nabla u|^2}+(u-1)^2\right)\,dx, \qquad u\in W^{1,2}_0(\Omega).

Square-integrability of the gradient does not itself give an integrable exponential. We therefore let E take values in [0,\infty]. The zero function has energy 2|\Omega|, so there is a finite starting point. The inequality e^r\geq r for r\geq0 controls the gradient, while convexity of z\mapsto e^{|z|^2} supplies lower semicontinuity. The direct method therefore gives a finite-energy minimizer among all fields in the same zero-boundary class, without a polynomial upper growth bound on the density.

The Sobolev counterpart of the quadratic L^2 model shows how these analytic inputs are discharged in practice: convexity, coercivity, and weak lower semicontinuity all follow from one identity.

Proof for Theorem 9.111
uses 1

The concrete integral equals the squared H^1 distance to g. Its weak lower semicontinuity and coercivity give a minimizer by the direct method; comparison with g forces the squared distance to vanish and hence proves uniqueness.

9.3.1.7.2. Scope of the integral theorem🔗

The boundary condition of the affine theorem is u-g\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega) for a given Sobolev field g. Because its compactness step uses only zero-boundary corrections, the theorem holds on every bounded measurable set in positive dimension, including dimension one.

Energies of vector-valued maps that depend on \det Du are not convex in the gradient. For them the lower-semicontinuity step goes through the weak continuity of the determinant instead, giving the polyconvex existence theorem, and the same continuity makes the pointwise constraint \det Du=1 weakly closed. Each further constraint needs its own proof that the admissible set is nonempty and weakly closed.

9.3.1.7.2.1. Example: the Dirichlet energy🔗

The prototypical application of the direct method is the Dirichlet energy

J(u)=\frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx-\int_\Omega f\,u\,dx, \qquad u\in H^1_0(\Omega),

where \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n\ge1, is a bounded open set and f\in L^2(\Omega). This energy governs the Poisson equation -\Delta u=f with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Its load term -f(x)s does not in general satisfy the pointwise lower bound uniform in s used by the extended mixed-energy theorem. Here Poincaré controls that term after integration. Let us trace the direct-method argument on H^1_0 through its four steps.

Step 1: Coercivity. The Poincaré inequality on H^1_0(\Omega) gives a constant C_P>0 with \|u\|_{L^2}\leq C_P\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}. Together with Cauchy–Schwarz and Young's inequality,

J(u)\geq\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2 -\|f\|_{L^2}\|u\|_{L^2} \geq\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2 -C_P\|f\|_{L^2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2} \geq\frac{1}{4}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2-C_P^2\|f\|_{L^2}^2.

Thus J(u)\to+\infty as \|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\to\infty, confirming coercivity.

Step 2: Bounded minimizing sequence. Let (u_k) be a minimizing sequence: J(u_k)\to\inf J. By coercivity, \|\nabla u_k\|_{L^2} is bounded. The Poincaré inequality then bounds \|u_k\|_{H^1_0}.

Step 3: Weak convergence and compactness. Since H^1_0(\Omega) is a reflexive Hilbert space, the Eberlein–Šmulian theorem extracts a subsequence u_{k_j}\rightharpoonup u weakly in H^1_0(\Omega). The gradient map is bounded and linear, so the gradients converge weakly in L^2 as well. These weak limits suffice for the two terms of this energy.

Step 4: Lower semicontinuity. The gradient term is convex and continuous in the strong H^1 norm, hence weakly lower semicontinuous:

\frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx \leq\liminf_{j\to\infty}\frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega|\nabla u_{k_j}|^2\,dx.

For the load term, Cauchy–Schwarz and Poincaré give |\int_\Omega f v|\leq C_P\|f\|_{L^2}\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}. Thus v\mapsto\int_\Omega f v is a bounded linear functional on H^1_0(\Omega) and is continuous for weak convergence. Therefore

J(u)\leq\liminf_{j\to\infty}J(u_{k_j})=\inf J.

Since u is admissible, J(u)=\inf J, and u is a minimizer.

Uniqueness. The energy J is strictly convex (the Hessian in direction v is \int|\nabla v|^2>0 for v\neq 0), so the minimizer is unique.

Euler–Lagrange equation. Stationarity DJ(u)[v]=0 for all v\in H^1_0 gives

\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega f\,v\,dx \qquad\text{for all }v\in H^1_0(\Omega),

which is the weak form of -\Delta u=f with u=0 on \partial\Omega. In the library, the zero-boundary Sobolev space, Dirichlet form, and load functional of this example come from the Poisson Dirichlet energy rather than from the integral-functional minimizer theorem.

At an unconstrained global minimizer of a Fréchet-differentiable real functional,

u\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}J \quad\Longrightarrow\quad DJ(u)=0\in H^*.

This is the Banach-space form of Evans's directional first-variation calculation. Variations that preserve boundary values need a constrained version, such as the mixed-density first-variation theorem.

Proof for Theorem 9.112
uses 0

Mathlib proves this for a local minimum, which every global minimum supplies. Its proof moves away from the minimizer along a fixed direction. Near a local minimum the difference quotients of the energy are nonnegative, and they converge to the first variation applied to that direction, so this value is nonnegative. The same bound for the opposite direction makes it zero. Since the direction was arbitrary, the first variation is the zero continuous linear map.

Let 1\leq p<\infty and let q be its Hölder conjugate. The theorem takes the full derivative dF(x,z) in the product state z=(s,\xi), with \|dF(x,z)\|\leq h(x)+C\|z\|^{p-1} and h\in L^q. Differentiability and the bound hold for every state outside a fixed null set. The density and the evaluated derivative (x,z,w)\mapsto dF(x,z)[w] are jointly measurable.

Suppose u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega) minimizes the nonnegative extended integral of F(x,u,\nabla u)+b(x) in the prescribed affine class and has finite energy. Here b is measurable and F(x,z)+b(x)\geq0 for every state outside a fixed null set. For every variation v in the supported smooth-core closure, the first-variation integrand dF(x,(u,\nabla u))[(v,\nabla v)] is integrable and has integral zero. On open sets this variation space is W^{1,p}_0(\Omega).

This necessary condition includes p=1,\ q=\infty, starting from a given finite minimum. The existence theorem uses p>1.

To see the differential equation inside this identity, write A=\partial_sF and D=\nabla_\xi F. Assume joint measurability and, almost everywhere in x, joint continuity of these partial derivatives in (s,\xi). Suppose they satisfy the conjugate growth bound with |A|+\|D\| in place of \|dF\|. Mathlib's product differentiation theorem assembles the full derivative:

dF(x,s,\xi)[r,z]=A(x,s,\xi)r+\langle D(x,s,\xi),z\rangle.

Substituting this expression into the first variation gives

\int_\Omega \left(A(x,u,\nabla u)v+ \langle D(x,u,\nabla u),\nabla v\rangle\right)\,dx=0.

This is the weak equation -\operatorname{div}D+A=0. The integral is finite for every admissible variation; no derivative of the integral functional is assumed.

    A finite extended-energy minimum in a prescribed affine Sobolev class satisfies an integrable weak first-variation identity for every zero-boundary Sobolev variation. The full density derivative has conjugate power growth on one common a.e. set. This includes p = 1, q = ∞ and assumes no derivative of the integral functional.

    Only the shifted density F + b must be nonnegative. Finiteness at the minimizer gives its integrability there, and derivative growth gives integrability along nearby variations. The spatial shift b need only be measurable.

    A finite minimum satisfies the weak equation -div D + A = 0 when A and D are the value and gradient derivatives of the density. Their joint continuity in the two state variables supplies the full derivative, and conjugate power growth makes its action on every zero-boundary Sobolev variation integrable.

    Each a.e. hypothesis holds simultaneously for every state. The endpoint p = 1, q = ∞ is included. The measurable shift b need not be integrable; only the shifted energy at the minimizer must be finite. No convexity or coercivity is required.

Proof for Theorem 9.113
uses 0

A common Hölder bound controls the line derivative for -1\leq t\leq1. The mean value theorem gives integrability of the shifted density along u+tv from its integrability at u. The nearby extended integrals can therefore be compared as real integrals and differentiated at t=0; minimality makes that derivative zero. This uses no separate upper growth bound on the density and does not require b itself to be integrable.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Under the same measurability, differentiability, shifted lower bound, finite-energy minimum, and finite-exponent growth hypotheses, collect the component states in Ju(x)=((u_k(x),\nabla u_k(x)))_k and allow F(x,Ju) to couple them. A shared minimum theorem gives \int_\Omega dF(x,Ju)[Jv]\,dx=0 for every vector variation in the zero-boundary class. The growth bound uses the maximum norm on the finite family of states.

    A finite extended-energy minimizer of a coupled density satisfies its weak Euler–Lagrange system against every vector-valued zero-boundary Sobolev variation. The full derivative has conjugate power growth on one common a.e. set.

    Boundary conditions are imposed componentwise in the supported smooth-core closure, which gives the usual affine W¹ᵖ₀ class on open sets. The result includes p = 1, q = ∞ and allows zero spatial dimension or an empty system. It needs no coercivity, upper growth bound on the density, or continuity of the derivative.

uses 0

The finite family of value-gradient pairs is in L^p. Apply the same dominated integral-differentiation argument to this product state. Every line u+tv remains in the componentwise affine class, so minimality makes the derivative vanish.

Let 1\le p\le\infty. Retain the measurable density and shift with F(x,z)+b(x)\ge0 almost everywhere for every state, and the same affine variation class. Write Ju=(u,\nabla u) for a member u of that class. Assume F(x,s,\xi) is jointly convex in (s,\xi) almost everywhere and has its actual derivative at Ju. Suppose the tested derivative is integrable and has integral zero for every admissible variation. Then u minimizes the shifted extended energy in that affine class. This follows from the tangent-plane inequality:

F(x,Jw)-F(x,Ju)\geq dF(x,Ju)[Jw-Ju].

    A weak solution minimizes a jointly convex mixed density in its affine Sobolev class. Here D(x) is the full derivative at (u(x), ∇u(x)), and the weak equation tests its value and gradient components together.

    Competitors may have infinite energy, and any finite-energy competitor forces the solution's energy to be finite. The domain is arbitrary, the dimension may be zero, and the Sobolev exponent may be 1 or ∞.

Proof for Theorem 9.115
uses 0

For a competitor in the same affine class, w-u is an admissible variation. The weak equation makes the integral on the right zero, giving the extended-energy comparison. An infinite-energy competitor is immediate; a finite-energy competitor also forces the solution's energy to be finite. This converse needs integrability of the tested derivative, but no power growth or coercivity, and it includes p=\infty with the supported-closure boundary class. Joint convexity matters here: the earlier existence argument only required convexity in the gradient.

Passing from the integrated identity DJ(u)[\varphi]=0 for all test directions to a pointwise Euler–Lagrange equation requires a localization principle.

uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let U\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and let f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be locally integrable on U for Lebesgue measure. If

\int_U f\,\varphi\,dx=0

for every smooth compactly supported \varphi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R whose support lies in U, then f vanishes almost everywhere on U:

f(x)=0\qquad\text{for almost every }x\in U.

Only the behavior of f inside U matters: each test function vanishes near the boundary and outside the domain. This is the localization step of Evans's Euler–Lagrange derivation in §8.1.2, which passes from the vanishing first variation to the almost-everywhere equation.

    If a function f locally integrable on an open subset U of a finite-dimensional real vector space has zero integral when multiplied by any smooth function compactly supported in U, then f vanishes almost everywhere in U.

There is a regularity step before applying this lemma to an energy density F(x,u,\nabla u). The first variation initially says

\int_U\bigl(D_pF(x,u,\nabla u)\cdot\nabla\varphi +D_uF(x,u,\nabla u)\varphi\bigr)=0.

If the flux D_pF has a weak divergence represented by a locally integrable function, and D_uF is locally integrable, integration by parts produces the locally integrable residual r=-\nabla\cdot D_pF+D_uF. The fundamental lemma then gives r=0 almost everywhere. Without that extra divergence regularity the displayed test identity still defines the distributional equation. Further regularity, such as continuity of r, is needed to conclude equality at every point.

Proof for Theorem 9.116
uses 0

Because every admissible \varphi is supported in U, the integral over U equals the integral over \mathbb R^n, so the hypothesis says that f integrates to zero against every smooth compactly supported function with support in the open set U. Mathlib's theorem for such functions then applies: smooth cutoffs supported in U approximate indicator functions of compact subsets of U, dominated convergence passes the vanishing integrals to those indicators, and a locally integrable function whose integral over every compact subset of U vanishes is zero almost everywhere on U.

9.3.1.7.3.1. A classical local minimum gives a pointwise equation🔗

The smooth version carries out each step of this bridge. It uses a neighborhood of the field in the uniform C^1 topology, rather than assuming that the first variation or the Euler–Lagrange residual vanishes. Write

J(u)=\int_\Omega L(Du(x),u(x),x)\,dx, \qquad u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m.

Here the matrix variable is first in the density L(P,z,x), unlike the earlier scalar notation F(x,s,p).

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and let u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^m). Assume L is jointly C^2 for x\in\Omega, with its values and its first two derivatives extending continuously to x\in\overline\Omega. Suppose some \varepsilon>0 satisfies

J(u)\le J(u+v)

for every globally C^2 perturbation v that vanishes on \partial\Omega and obeys \|v(x)\|+\|Dv(x)\|<\varepsilon on \overline\Omega. The Jacobian norm here is the elementwise supremum norm. Then at every x\in\Omega and for every component k,

-\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_i \left(L_{P_{ki}}(Du,u,x)\right)+L_{z_k}(Du,u,x)=0.

The minimizer is assumed to be C^2, and the equation is a necessary condition for it.

    A uniform C¹ local minimizer satisfies the full coupled Euler–Lagrange system at every interior point. Smooth compactly supported tests have zero boundary values, and their scalar multiples eventually lie in the minimizing neighborhood.

Proof for Theorem 9.117
uses 0

Fix a smooth compactly supported variation v in \Omega. Compactness of \overline\Omega bounds both v and Dv, so u+tv lies in the minimizing neighborhood for sufficiently small |t|. The function t\mapsto J(u+tv) therefore has derivative zero at zero. The continuous second jet supplies the bounds needed to differentiate under the integral. Integration by parts transfers the derivatives of v to the flux, with no boundary term. The fundamental lemma makes each Euler–Lagrange component zero almost everywhere; its continuity upgrades this to every interior point.

9.3.1.7.3.2. From a variational symmetry to a conserved current🔗

A symmetry can move the field and the spatial coordinates together. Let \Phi_t(y) move space and let \Psi_t(y,z) transform field values. The transformed field is defined near a point by its graph,

U_t(\Phi_t(y))=\Psi_t(y,u(y)).

The Jacobian determinant in a change of variables matters: invariance of the action density means invariance of L(DU_t,U_t,\cdot)\det D\Phi_t, not merely of L at the original coordinates. The theorem constructs U_t by local inversion of \Phi_t and differentiates this finite invariance.

Fix x. Assume u is C^2 at x, L is jointly C^2 at (Du(x),u(x),x), and the maps (t,y)\mapsto\Phi_t(y) and (t,y,z)\mapsto\Psi_t(y,z) are jointly C^2 at (0,x) and (0,x,u(x)), respectively. Near x, suppose \Phi_0(y)=y and \Psi_0(y,u(y))=u(y). For the locally induced field U_t, assume that for all sufficiently small t,

L(DU_t(\Phi_t(x)),\Psi_t(x,u(x)),\Phi_t(x))\det D\Phi_t(x) =L(Du(x),u(x),x).

If u satisfies the Euler–Lagrange system at x, define X(y)=\partial_t\Phi_t(y)|_{t=0} and \eta(y)=\partial_t\Psi_t(y,u(y))|_{t=0}. Then the current

J_i=\sum_k L_{P_{ki}}(Du,u,y)\bigl(\eta-Du\,X\bigr)_k +L(Du,u,y)X_i

satisfies \operatorname{div}J(x)=0. All hypotheses are local at the specified points; a global inverse or a transformation group is not required.

Invariance is equality of densities with the spatial Jacobian determinant. The resulting current is expressed entirely in the original field and the parameter derivatives of Φ and Ψ.

Proof for Theorem 9.118
uses 0

At parameter zero, D\Phi_0(x)=I. The inverse function theorem constructs a jointly C^2 induced field satisfying the graph identity. Differentiating that identity at fixed spatial coordinates gives the field variation \eta-Du\,X. Differentiating the finite density invariance also gives the volume term L\operatorname{div}X. The product and chain rules assemble these terms into the divergence of the displayed current, plus the Euler–Lagrange residual paired with the field variation. That residual vanishes at x, leaving conservation of the current.

9.3.2. Second Variations and Dirichlet Energy🔗

Evans derives first- and second-variation tests for integral functionals on pp. 454–459 by restricting the energy to affine lines.

The first variation detects a critical point. It cannot distinguish a minimum from a maximum or saddle. The second variation supplies the next test. If u is a local minimizer and \varphi is an admissible direction, the one-dimensional function

g(t)=J(u+t\varphi)

has a local minimum at t=0. Therefore g'(0)=0 and g''(0)\geq0. Fréchet differentiation identifies these derivatives with DJ(u)[\varphi] and D^2J(u)[\varphi,\varphi].

Nonnegativity is only a necessary test in this generality: both J(s)=s^4 and J(s)=-s^4 have zero first and second derivatives at zero, although one has a minimum and the other a maximum. Quadratic energies are more informative because their expansion has no unexamined higher-order remainder.

uses 0

9.3.2.2. Nonlinear integral functionals🔗

For J(u)=\int_\Omega L(Du,u,x)\,dx, the second variation has gradient, field, and mixed terms. The gradient term can be isolated by variations that oscillate rapidly in a fixed direction. This tests the matrix Hessian only on rank-one matrices, the matrices produced by differentiating one scalar oscillation times one vector amplitude.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be bounded and open and u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^m). Assume L(P,z,x) is jointly C^2 for x\in\Omega, with its values and first two derivatives extending continuously to x\in\overline\Omega. If t\mapsto J(u+tv) has a local minimum at zero for a globally C^2 variation v, then

\delta^2J(u)[v,v]=\int_\Omega D^2L(Du,u,x)[(Dv,v,0),(Dv,v,0)]\,dx\ge0.

If this local-minimum condition holds for every smooth compactly supported vector variation in \Omega, then at every x\in\Omega,

D^2_{PP}L(Du(x),u(x),x)[a\otimes\xi,a\otimes\xi]\ge0 \qquad(a\in\mathbb R^m,\ \xi\in(\mathbb R^n)^*).

The domain needs no boundary regularity. The pointwise condition tests the matrix Hessian on rank-one directions only, and it is necessary for a minimum but not sufficient.

    A classical local minimizer has a nonnegative matrix Hessian on every rank-one direction at every interior point. The local-minimum hypothesis is the same one used for the first-order Euler–Lagrange condition, with compactly supported smooth vector variations. No positivity, stationarity, or second-derivative identity is assumed.

Proof for Theorem 9.121
uses 0

Differentiate J(u+tv) twice under the integral using the continuous second jet. The scalar second-derivative test gives the integral inequality. Next fix a smooth cutoff g supported in \Omega and use the pair v_s(y)=g(y)a\sin(\lambda\xi(y)) and v_c(y)=g(y)a\cos(\lambda\xi(y)). Adding their second variations cancels the mixed oscillatory terms and gives A+\lambda^2 B\ge0 for every real \lambda, where

B=\int_\Omega g^2 D^2_{PP}L(Du,u,y)[a\otimes\xi,a\otimes\xi]\,dy.

Hence B\ge0. If the continuous rank-one Hessian were negative at an interior point, a nonzero cutoff in a neighborhood where it stays negative would give B<0. This local contradiction proves the pointwise condition.

Proof for Theorem 9.123
uses 1

Mathlib's bilinear derivative rule differentiates B(u,u). Symmetry combines the two resulting terms, while the load differentiates to itself.

At a local minimizer the derivative vanishes by Fermat's theorem, and the derivative formula turns that vanishing into an identity in every direction. Because the energy is quadratic in u, no separate differentiability hypothesis is needed here, in contrast to the semilinear energies, where differentiability of the potential has to be supplied before a minimizer can be called a weak solution.

Proof for Theorem 9.124
uses 1

Fermat's theorem makes the derivative vanish at a local minimum. Substituting the derivative formula and evaluating the zero functional gives the weak equation.

The Euler equation used only the first derivative. The second derivative is where the quadratic structure pays off: because DJ(u) depends affinely on u, the Hessian does not depend on the base point at all, and the second-variation test can be evaluated without knowing the minimizer.

9.3.2.4. Dirichlet Energy and Poisson's Equation🔗

For the symmetric quadratic energy J(w)=\frac12B(w,w)-\ell(w), stationarity at u gives B(u,v)=\ell(v). Expanding at that point therefore yields

J(u+v)-J(u)=\frac12B(v,v).

If B(v,v)\geq c\|v\|^2 with c>0, an energy gap bounds the squared distance to the minimizer by 2/c times that gap. This is a useful connection to certified computation: a certified energy estimate becomes a field-error estimate once coercivity and admissibility in the same space have been established.

For f\in L^2(\Omega), the Poisson Dirichlet energy on H^1_0(\Omega) is the quadratic energy built from the Dirichlet form and the load functional of f. The abstract Hessian formula specializes to it without any new computation.

uses 1

Specialize the quadratic Hessian formula to the symmetric Dirichlet form and the continuous load induced by the forcing term.

On the diagonal the Dirichlet form is a sum of squared L^2 norms of weak derivatives, so the necessary condition D^2J(u)[v,v]\geq0 holds for every v whether or not u is a minimizer. The second-variation test never rules out a critical point of the Dirichlet energy.

Proof for Theorem 9.129
uses 1

The forward direction is the local first-variation condition. Conversely, the Dirichlet principle makes every weak solution a global minimizer, hence a local minimizer.

9.3.3. Null Lagrangians and Constraints🔗

Convexity in the full gradient is too restrictive for many elastic energies. An energy that penalizes compression can depend on \det Du, which is not convex as a function of matrices in dimension at least two. The polyconvex densities treated here depend convexly on the gradient and its determinant as separate variables. To pass to a weak limit, we must then identify the limiting determinant: for q>n the determinant is continuous from the weak topology of W^{1,q} to the weak topology of L^{q/n}. Its null-Lagrangian structure supplies this fact.

Constraints require a separate weak-closedness argument. The same determinant continuity preserves \det Du=1; strong L^2 compactness preserves |u|=1. Neither admissible class is generally convex. These are the constrained variational problems developed in Evans Evans (2010), Chapter 8.

9.3.3.1. Null Lagrangians🔗

For a density L(P,z,x) of a map u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m, with P standing for Du and z for u, the Euler–Lagrange expression in component k is

-\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_i\Bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial P_{ki}}(Du,u,x)\Bigr) +\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_k}(Du,u,x).

Usually this expression vanishes only for the critical points of the action \int_\Omega L(Du,u,x)\,dx. A null Lagrangian is a density for which it vanishes for every map.

A density L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R is a null Lagrangian on \Omega if every smooth map u on \Omega satisfies the Euler–Lagrange system, with classical derivatives, at every point of \Omega. The determinant density is L(P,z,x)=\det P on square matrices.

Proof for Theorem 9.131
uses 0

The derivative of \det in the entry (k,i) is the cofactor (\operatorname{cof}P)_{ki}, at singular matrices as well, and the density does not depend on z. The Euler–Lagrange expression is therefore -\sum_i\partial_i(\operatorname{cof}Du)_{ki}, and the rows of the cofactor matrix of a C^2 map are divergence free. This is the Piola identity. Each cofactor is a sum of products of first derivatives, and after differentiation the mixed second derivatives cancel in pairs.

The name is explained by what the action does. If the Euler–Lagrange expression vanishes identically, the derivative of the action along any path of maps with fixed boundary values is zero, so the action depends only on the boundary values.

Let L be a null Lagrangian on an open set \Omega with C^2 joint dependence on its arguments. Then every C^2 map on \Omega also satisfies its Euler–Lagrange system. If \Omega is bounded with C^2 graph boundary and L has a continuous second jet, then two maps that are C^2 up to the boundary, continuous on \overline\Omega, and equal on \partial\Omega have the same action

\int_\Omega L(Du,u,x)\,dx=\int_\Omega L(Dv,v,x)\,dx.

Proof for Theorem 9.132
uses 0

The Euler–Lagrange expression at a point depends only on the second jet of the map there, and every second jet is realized by a polynomial map, which is smooth. This passes the null property from smooth maps to C^2 maps. For the action, extend u and v across the boundary to C^2 maps on the whole space, using reflection in the graph charts, and consider w_t=(1-t)u+tv. The first-variation identity writes \frac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega L(Dw_t,w_t,x)\,dx as the integral of the Euler–Lagrange expression of w_t against v-u, plus a boundary term that vanishes because v-u=0 on \partial\Omega. The Euler–Lagrange expression is zero, so the action is constant in t.

9.3.3.2. Polyconvex energies🔗

Write W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n) for maps whose n components lie in W^{1,q}(\Omega). A polyconvex density of the kind proved here has the form L(Du,u,x)=F(x,u,Du,\det Du), where F(x,s,P,d) is convex in the pair (P,d) jointly but can be far from convex in P alone. The standard example is |P|^q+\varphi(\det P) with \varphi convex. The integral is taken in the extended sense, so it may be +\infty, and only a lower bound on the graph d=\det P is required.

Lower semicontinuity comes from separating the two arguments. When u_k\rightharpoonup u weakly in W^{1,q} with q>n, the gradients converge weakly in L^q, and by the null-Lagrangian structure the determinants converge weakly in L^{q/n}. The pair (Du_k,\det Du_k) therefore converges weakly to (Du,\det Du), and a functional that is convex in a weakly converging variable is weakly lower semicontinuous.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n\ge1, be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and let q>n be real. Let F(x,s,P,d) be C^1 on \Omega\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^{n\times n}\times\mathbb R, convex in (P,d) for each x\in\Omega and s, and bounded below by -\beta on the graph d=\det P. If u_k\rightharpoonup u weakly in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n), then

\int_\Omega F(x,u,Du,\det Du)\,dx \le\liminf_{k\to\infty}\int_\Omega F(x,u_k,Du_k,\det Du_k)\,dx.

Proof for Theorem 9.133
uses 0

Lift each map to the pair (Du_k,\det Du_k), with values in \mathbb R^{n\times n+1}. Weak convergence of the determinants, from W^{1,q} to L^{q/n}, makes the lifted sequence converge weakly. The mixed convex lower semicontinuity theorem for integrands convex in a weakly converging variable and continuous in a strongly converging one then applies, with the values u_k converging strongly by compact embedding.

With lower semicontinuity in hand, the direct method goes through.

Under the hypotheses of the lower semicontinuity theorem, suppose also that \alpha|P|^q-\beta\le F(x,s,P,\det P) with \alpha>0 and \beta of either sign. For every boundary datum \gamma whose trace class

A=\{u\in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n): u=\gamma\text{ on }\partial\Omega\text{ in the trace sense}\}

is nonempty, the extended energy \int_\Omega F(x,u,Du,\det Du)\,dx attains its minimum on A. The same holds for an affine class g+W^{1,q}_0. If some member of A has finite energy, the minimizer's density is integrable and its energy is an ordinary real integral.

    A single finite-energy admissible map gives a minimizer whose original density is integrable. Its signed extended energy is its ordinary real integral, and it still minimizes against the entire trace class, including infinite-energy competitors.

Proof for Theorem 9.134
uses 0

A nonempty trace class is the affine class g+W^{1,q}_0 of any of its members. If every competitor has infinite energy, any member minimizes. Otherwise the coercivity bound makes a minimizing sequence bounded in W^{1,q}, reflexivity extracts a weakly convergent subsequence, the affine class is weakly closed, and lower semicontinuity shows that the limit minimizes.

9.3.3.3. Constrained minimization🔗

A constraint J(u)=c given by a differentiable functional is the simplest case, and the finite-dimensional rule survives in a Banach space: at a constrained extremum the derivative of the energy is a multiple of the derivative of the constraint, provided that the constraint derivative is nonzero and both functionals have the strict differentiability required below.

Let E be a real Banach space and F,J:E\to\mathbb R strictly differentiable at u, with J'(u)\ne0. If u is a local extremum of F on the level set \{v:J(v)=J(u)\}, then F'(u)=\lambda J'(u) for some \lambda\in\mathbb R.

    At a constrained local extremum with nonzero constraint derivative, the objective derivative is a scalar multiple of the constraint derivative.

Proof for Theorem 9.135
uses 0

The implicit function argument gives coefficients (a,b)\ne(0,0) with aJ'(u)+bF'(u)=0. If b were zero then a\ne0 and J'(u)=0, which is excluded. Take \lambda=-a/b.

The incompressibility constraint \det Du=1 is pointwise, not a single level set, and no multiplier rule is needed for existence. Weak continuity of the determinant does the work: if \det Du_k=1 almost everywhere and u_k\rightharpoonup u in W^{1,q}, q>n, then \det Du_k\rightharpoonup\det Du in L^{q/n}, and a weak limit of the constant function 1 is 1. The admissible class is weakly closed although it is not convex.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n\ge1, be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, let q>n, and let L(x,s,P) be C^1, convex in P, with \alpha|P|^q-\beta\le L(x,s,P) for some \alpha>0. If g\in W^{1,q}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n) has \det Dg=1 almost everywhere, the extended energy \int_\Omega L(x,u,Du)\,dx attains its minimum among maps u\in g+W^{1,q}_0 with \det Du=1 almost everywhere. When L=L(x,P) does not depend on the value, the same holds in the class of maps with trace \gamma and \det Du=1, for every boundary datum \gamma for which that class is nonempty; if one admissible map has finite energy, the minimizer's density is integrable and its energy is finite.

        fun x z ↦

    If one admissible map has finite energy, the determinant-constrained minimizer has an integrable density and its signed energy equals the ordinary real integral. It still minimizes over the whole admissible class.

Proof for Theorem 9.136
uses 0

Run the direct method in the affine class of the given admissible map. The constraint set is weakly sequentially closed by the weak continuity of the determinant, and the energy is weakly lower semicontinuous because it is convex in Du. A bounded minimizing sequence in the constraint set has a weak limit that stays in it.

The sphere constraint |u|=1 is the other classical example. Strong L^2 compactness preserves unit length and gives a minimizer when the admissible class is nonempty. Deriving its equation needs a different argument. A variation U+tV leaves the sphere, so it is projected back: the variation is G(U+tV), where G is a smooth map that agrees with z\mapsto z/|z| on the annulus \tfrac12\le|z|\le2. For a bounded direction V and small |t|, U+tV stays in that annulus and the projected map again has unit length and the same boundary values.

uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^{n+1} be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary. Choose a smooth compactly supported map G:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m agreeing with z/|z| on \tfrac12\le|z|\le2. Let U\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m) have |U|=1 almost everywhere and let V\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m) be bounded by M. For |t|M<\tfrac12 the projected variation G(U+tV) has unit length almost everywhere, and if V\in H^1_0 it has the boundary values of U. The Dirichlet energy E(W)=\tfrac12\int_\Omega|DW|^2 of the projected variation is differentiable at t=0 with derivative

\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}E\bigl(G(U+tV)\bigr) =\int_\Omega\Bigl(DU:DV-|DU|^2\,U\cdot V\Bigr)\,dx.

    Composing an affine zero-boundary variation with a cutoff of normalization preserves the original boundary values for every parameter.

Proof for Theorem 9.137
uses 0

The graph-domain hypotheses supply the Sobolev extension operator and inward partition used for composition and preservation of the boundary values. The smooth compactly supported cutoff has bounded derivative and Lipschitz DG. Since |U|=1, the chain rule gives D(G(U+tV))=DG(U+tV)\,(DU+tDV), and at t=0 the derivative of the normalization z\mapsto z/|z| at a unit vector is the projection I-z\otimes z. Differentiating |U|^2=1 gives (DU)^TU=0, which turns the projected term into -|DU|^2U\cdot V. Differentiation under the integral sign is justified by an integrable bound built from the Lipschitz bound on DG.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^{n+1} be bounded and open with C^1 graph boundary, and let g\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m). Assume the class

\mathcal A_g=\{W\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m): |W|=1\text{ a.e.},\ W-g\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\}

is nonempty. Then the Dirichlet energy attains its minimum on \mathcal A_g. Every such minimizer U satisfies

\int_\Omega DU:DV\,dx=\int_\Omega|DU|^2\,U\cdot V\,dx \qquad\text{for every }V\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\cap L^\infty.

This is the weak form of the harmonic map equation -\Delta U=|DU|^2U. Nonemptiness of \mathcal A_g is a hypothesis.

    A nonempty sphere-valued boundary class on a bounded C¹ graph domain (such a domain is open) has a Dirichlet minimizer satisfying the nonlinear weak harmonic-map equation. The equation is derived from the constructed minimum by normalized admissible variations; no first-variation identity or additional regularity is assumed.

    A sphere-valued Dirichlet minimizer satisfies the weak harmonic-map equation against every bounded zero-boundary Sobolev field.

Proof for Theorem 9.138
uses 0

For existence, an energy-bounded minimizing sequence has bounded gradients. Poincaré's inequality controls the zero-boundary differences from g, so weak compactness gives an H^1 limit with the same boundary values. Rellich compactness gives strong L^2 convergence, preserving unit length almost everywhere, and weak lower semicontinuity gives minimality. This existence argument itself needs only a bounded open domain of positive dimension.

For the equation, the projected variations are admissible competitors, so the energy along them has a minimum at t=0 and its derivative there vanishes. The previous theorem computes that derivative. An essentially bounded test field has an almost-everywhere bound M, which is all the variation theorem asks for, and the graph boundary supplies the Sobolev extension that the composition with G needs.

The multiplier in the harmonic map equation is |DU|^2, a function rather than a number. Formally it is the multiplier for a constraint imposed at every point; here it comes out of the projected variation directly.

9.3.3.4. Contact with an obstacle🔗

An inequality constraint changes the Euler equation precisely where the minimizer touches the obstacle. Consider

J(v)=\frac12\int_\Omega |Dv|^2\,dx-\int_\Omega fv\,dx, \qquad v\in H^1_0(\Omega),\quad v\ge\psi\text{ a.e.}

Upward variations are admissible at contact, while downward ones may not be. The resulting reaction r=-\Delta u-f is nonnegative. Away from contact both directions become available and the Poisson equation is recovered. Starting from a constrained minimizer, the regularity theorem supplies the extra differentiability needed to express this description almost everywhere.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be bounded and open with C^2 graph boundary. Let f\in L^2(\Omega) and let the obstacle \psi be C^2 up to the boundary, continuous on \overline\Omega, and nonpositive on \partial\Omega. If u\in H^1_0(\Omega) minimizes J among fields above \psi, then u has an H^2 representative U. Its reaction obeys

0\le r=-\Delta U-f\le(-\Delta\psi-f)^+,\qquad r(U-\psi)=0 \quad\text{a.e. in }\Omega.

On the contact set U=\psi, one has \Delta U=\Delta\psi almost everywhere; on U>\psi, one has -\Delta U=f almost everywhere.

    Classical C² obstacle data with the boundary sign required by the homogeneous Dirichlet condition imply global H² regularity, the reaction bound, complementarity, and the contact and noncontact equations for every obstacle minimizer. All boundary infrastructure is derived from geometry.

Proof for Theorem 9.139
uses 1

The graph boundary supplies the extension and trace infrastructure. The classical obstacle defines an H^2 field whose Sobolev trace agrees with its boundary values, so the boundary sign becomes the sign condition needed by the obstacle regularity theorem. The constrained variational inequality and its reaction estimate then give the H^2 lift and 0\le r\le(-\Delta\psi-f)^+. Complementarity sets the reaction to zero off contact. On contact, the Sobolev derivatives of U-\psi vanish almost everywhere on its zero set, giving equality of the Laplacians.

9.3.4. Regularity of Local Minimizers🔗

The direct method produces a minimizer in a Sobolev space, and the first variation makes it a weak solution of its Euler–Lagrange equation. How regular is it? For an energy

I(u)=\int_\Omega F(\nabla u)\,dx, \qquad \theta|\xi|^2\leq D^2F(p)[\xi,\xi]\leq\Lambda|\xi|^2,\quad\theta>0,

the answer is: as regular as the density allows. Evans treats the first steps in Section 8.3 Evans (2010). The main step, Hölder continuity of the first derivatives, is the theorem of De Giorgi and Nash Giorgi (1957) Nash (1958). Analyticity of sufficiently regular solutions goes back to Bernstein, in two variables Bernstein (1904). Later proofs cover any dimension and systems, among them Morrey's for nonlinear elliptic systems Morrey (1958).

The statements below hold in every dimension and on every open set. Nothing is assumed at the boundary, and the minimizer is only locally in W^{1,2}.

✓L∃∀N

A function u is a local minimizer of \int F(\nabla u) on \Omega if, on every open set V with compact closure in \Omega, adding a smooth function with compact support in V does not lower the energy over V:

\int_V F(\nabla u)\,dx\leq\int_V F(\nabla u+\nabla\varphi)\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(V).

The condition is stated for the W^{1,2}(V) representatives of u. The regularity theorems add the hypothesis that u is locally in W^{1,2}.

    def PDE.CalculusOfVariations.IsLocalMinimizerOn
  {n : ℕ} (F : ℝ^n → ℝ) (Ω : Set ℝ^n)
  (u : ℝ^n → ℝ) : Prop

    u is a local minimizer of ∫ F(∇u) on Ω: on every open V with compact closure in Ω, every W^{1,2}(V) element that represents u has no more energy than its perturbation by any smooth function with compact support in V.

    The perturbations may be large, and they are the smallest class in use, so among the notions that compare with all perturbations in a class this is the weakest. Nothing is asked of u outside such sets V, and Ω need not be bounded.

    The predicate does not say that u is in W^{1,2}_loc(Ω): on a set V where u has no representative in W^{1,2}(V) it asks nothing. It does not say that the energies are finite either: the integrals are Bochner integrals, which are 0 for a density that is not integrable. The regularity theorems assume IsLocallyWkpOn 1 2 Ω u and a density with Lipschitz gradient, for which every energy is finite (integrable_gradientDensity_of_lipschitzWith).

The perturbation may be large, and smooth functions with compact support are the smallest class of competitors in use. So among the notions that compare u with all perturbations in a class, this is the weakest. For the densities above, a minimizer with prescribed boundary values on a bounded open set is a local minimizer, and so is every affine function.

For every dimension n and all constants \theta>0 and \Lambda there is an exponent \gamma\in(0,1) with the following property.     Hölder continuous gradient of local minimizers (De Giorgi–Nash regularity). In every dimension n and for all θ > 0 and Λ there is an exponent γ in (0, 1) with the following property. Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be open, let F be C² with θ ‖ξ‖² ≤ D²F(p)(ξ, ξ) ≤ Λ ‖ξ‖² for all p and ξ, and let u in W^{1,2}_loc(Ω) be a local minimizer of ∫ F(∇u). Then u has a representative v that is C¹ on Ω, and every point of Ω is the centre of a ball on which ∇v is Hölder continuous with exponent γ.

    This is the first step of the regularity theory of minimizers (De Giorgi, Nash): a C² density gives C^{1,γ} locally. The Hölder condition is stated for the gradient as a map into ℝⁿ. The statement is exists_contDiffOn_one_of_isLocalMinimizerOn together with exists_holder_exponent_gradient_of_isLocalMinimizerOn.

Proof for Theorem 9.141
uses 0

On a small ball the minimizer is a weak solution of \operatorname{div}(\nabla F(\nabla u))=0. Difference quotients give second weak derivatives, and each first derivative solves a linear equation whose coefficients D^2F(\nabla u) are bounded, elliptic and merely measurable. The theorem of De Giorgi and Nash makes it Hölder continuous. The representatives on balls agree on overlaps and glue.

Proof for Theorem 9.142
uses 1

Once the gradient is Hölder continuous, so are the coefficients D^2F(\nabla u) of the linearized equation. Schauder estimates then give one more derivative of u for each further derivative of F.

Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n be open and let F be real-analytic on \mathbb R^n with the two bounds. Every local minimizer u\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega) has a representative that is real-analytic on \Omega and solves \operatorname{div}(\nabla F(\nabla v))=0 there. Conversely, a function with such a representative is locally in W^{1,2} and is a local minimizer.

    Local minimizers are exactly the analytic solutions. Let Ω ⊆ ℝⁿ be open and let F be real-analytic on ℝⁿ with θ ‖ξ‖² ≤ D²F(p)(ξ, ξ) ≤ Λ ‖ξ‖² for all p and ξ, where θ > 0. A function u is in W^{1,2}_loc(Ω) and is a local minimizer of ∫ F(∇u) on Ω if and only if it agrees almost everywhere on Ω with a function that is real-analytic on Ω and satisfies div(∇F(∇v)) = 0 at every point of Ω.

    One direction is exists_analytic_of_isLocalMinimizerOn. The other is isLocalMinimizerOn_iff_exists_smooth, since an analytic function is smooth.

Proof for Theorem 9.143

Theorem 9.142
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

The smooth representative of the previous theorem solves the Euler–Lagrange equation at every point, so the next theorem applies to it. The converse holds because F is convex: a classical solution minimizes.

A continuous local minimizer is its own representative, so it is analytic as it stands. The step from smooth to analytic does not use minimality. It is a statement about smooth solutions of the equation.

Theorem9.144
Group: Regularity of local minimizers of gradient energies (4)

Definition 9.140

uses 0used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let u be smooth on an open set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n with \operatorname{div}(\nabla F(\nabla u))=0 there. If F is real-analytic at the gradients \nabla u(x), x\in\Omega, and D^2F is positive definite at these gradients, then u is real-analytic on \Omega. More generally, a smooth solution v=(v_l) of a system

\sum_i\partial_i\Bigl(\sum_j a_{ij}(v)\,\partial_jv_l-f_{li}(v)\Bigr)=0

is real-analytic when a_{ij} and f_{li} are real-analytic at the values of v and the matrix a(v(x)) is positive definite at every point.

Proof for Theorem 9.144
uses 0

The gradient of u solves a system of the second kind with a_{ij}=\partial_j\partial_iF. For such a system we show |D^iv|\leq i!\,MK^i near each point, which makes the Taylor series converge. Fix a ball with weight \eta(x)=R^2-|x-x_0|^2 and consider \eta^{2j}|D^jv|^2+\mu\,\eta^{2j-2}|D^{j-1}v|^2. At an interior maximum the operator with coefficients frozen at that point is nonpositive on it, while a Bernstein-type inequality bounds the operator from below by the derivatives of order j+1 and j. The derivatives of the equation are estimated by the Leibniz rule and a majorant form of the chain rule, with a weight on the Taylor coefficients that is closed under convolution. The result is a bound that improves itself: if the weighted derivatives are at most 2M times the target, they are at most M times the target. Since finitely many derivatives are bounded on the closed ball, this gives the bounds for all orders with one pair of constants. The plan, weighted derivatives and a recursion that absorbs the top order, follows Blatt Blatt (2024), with sup norms and the maximum principle in place of his L^2 estimates.

Armstrong and Kempe formalized the De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory for linear equations with bounded measurable coefficients in Lean Armstrong and Kempe (2026). The theorems here concern minimizers of nonlinear energies and use the library's own form of the De Giorgi step.
